lines: PRESIDENT:  Good morning, everybody.  Good morning both
counsel Mr Stephen, Mr Luke.  Yes.  Well, as part of
housekeeping, if you like, I need to indicate that
given the circumstances for the situation and conflict
situation in the Gulf, Arabian Gulf region, and this
is why we're having this hearing online, instead of
having it in London or in Bahrain.
There is a strong view, at least from the, one of
the tribunal member, that if the situation escalated,
for God bidden, whether in Bahrain or UAE, where I
guess both co-arbitrators -- I am based in London
anyway, but for my co arbitrator, so Dr Abdulla in
Bahrain and Mr Adrian in Abu Dhabi, if I'm not wrong,
if the situation escalated -- and I think some of the
counsel is based in Bahrain, and witness as well --
there is kind of possibility to adjourn this hearing,
wherever we're going to stop in any day during the
hearing.
I hope this is not the case, but I just want to
put you on notice that if anything escalated and the
tribunal member or the expert or the counsel will not
be able to continue, then there is no other option
rather than to adjourn the rest of the final hearing
for another day or another, another week.  I hope I
made myself clear.
MR BURKE:  Yes, sir.
MR WYGAS:  Yes, sir.
PRESIDENT:  Excellent.  Now, the second point I would
like to raise, that -- two points actually.  The first
one is regarding the list of issue, which is we
received, I think, a draft on 25th May.  There is no
any update on that draft, right?
MR BURKE:  It was agreed, sir, I think on the afternoon
of 26th May.  So the version that was circulated in
the afternoon of 26th May, my understanding is an
agreed list of issues.
PRESIDENT:  Yes.  Counsel Luke, same thing.
I think you are muted.
MR WYGAS:  Yes, sir.  That's right.  The list of issues
is agreed.
PRESIDENT:  Perfect.
Now, the second point regarding the application
made by the respondent on the 5th -- on 18th May,
which was the chairman birthday, which is a good day.
Of course, we'll give now the opportunity for the --
to start with the respondent, because this is his
application.  And then for the claimant reply.  Then
the tribunal going to go for the breaking room to
discuss this application and how we're going to deal
with it.  Then we'll come back to you.  Is that all
right?
MR BURKE:  Yes, I think on the current timetable --
PRESIDENT:  Yes.
MR BURKE:  -- the running order for today is housekeeping
and then the application.  And then I think we are due
to take a break for 15 minutes.
Of course, if the tribunal needs longer than
15 minutes, we can just send a message on the Zoom
platform and we can rejoin, as necessary.
PRESIDENT:  Yes.  Now, any housekeeping from both, both
of you, before we start the application?
MR BURKE:  There was one point regarding powers of
attorney.  I don't know whether the tribunal wants to
deal with that now or deal with that at the end.  It's
a straight point.  There's a point on my parameter
anyway, and a point I think on my learned friend's.
PRESIDENT:  Any view from the other side?
MR WYGAS:  It would probably be better to deal with the
power of attorney at the outset.
PRESIDENT:  Yeah.  Tribunal member, any comments?
DR TALEB:  I'm fine.
PRESIDENT:  Shall we deal with that later?
MR COLE:  I'm fine for it to be dealt with first,
actually, I think it's probably good to get it out of
the way.
PRESIDENT:  Okay.
DR TALEB:  Agree, agree.
MR BURKE:  It is a simple point, I think, on both sides.
The first is that my power of attorney, there is a
suggestion it has been given to me in my capacity
formerly as a partner at Addleshaw Goddard, and that
now I am at 39 Essex Chambers, it no longer applies.
We don't think that's right.  We don't think
that's what the power of attorney says.  But of
course, if the tribunal would like us to issue a new
power of attorney that ratifies everything done in the
intervening period since I ceased being a partner at
Addleshaw Goddard and began practice at the bar, we're
very happy to do that.  We couldn't do that last week,
of course, because it was only raised, I think, in the
middle of the Eid holiday.  But we can do that, if
necessary.
The point, with my learned friend's -- is simply
the date of it.  It was issued after the written
submissions were filed, and it doesn't contain any
retrospective ratification of acts prior to its date.
Now, he may say: ah, but it's also signed -- the
written submissions are also signed by Trowers &
Hamlins, and they do have a power of attorney.
My difficulty with that is that the power of
attorney given to Trowers & Hamlins is given to named
individuals, and there is no named individual who
signed the written submissions.
So I accept it as an abundance of caution.  But
given that we are being required or may be required to
reissue our power of attorney in any event, it seems
sensible that the respondent does likewise.
PRESIDENT:  Yes.  Mr Luke.
MR WYGAS:  Yes, sir.  I can deal with that quickly in
relation to the claimant's power of attorney, we can
see that at B1.2.  I don't know if that's being
brought up.  {B1.2-1}.  That's right, I think.
And you can now see, if we just make that slightly
larger:
"TTSJV hereby authorises and empowers each of..."
The first being Mr Burke.
And then after that:
"... and any other attorney, lawyer or legal
consultant of Addleshaw Goddard..."
Therefore, we say that the power of attorney is
clearly limited to attorneys, lawyers or legal
consultants of Addleshaw Goddard, four having been
named, and therefore it is appropriate and right that
Mr Burke, now not being an attorney, lawyer or legal
consultant of Addleshaw Goddard, provides a further
power of attorney.
PRESIDENT:  Yes.  I might invite my co-arbitrator to make
any comments on this.  Mr Adrian, probably.
MR COLE:  Yeah, I'd just ask the question: do we actually
need a power of attorney?  I mean, as I understand the
rules, and I haven't checked immediately, the tribunal
just has to be satisfied that the representatives of
the parties are duly authorised.
The mere fact they are in attendance today must
indicate that, rather than actually having a
prescribed form of authorisation.  Perhaps the parties
would just like to comment on that point.
MR BURKE:  I think that's entirely right, sir, that 18,
I think it's relating, one of the LCIA rules simply
requires parties to provide such proof of authority as
the tribunal may require.  As I have said, if the
tribunal requires further proof than this power of
attorney we're happy to provide it.  We don't think
it's required.  We don't think it's required under the
rules or indeed under the power of attorney.
But in an abundance of caution, if the tribunal
would like us to have a new power of attorney issued,
we're happy to do that.
MR WYGAS:  In response to that, I would simply say
further down the line, the matter is not one for this
tribunal, but it's one for the Bahraini courts.  And
I think all parties understand that in relation to
Bahraini courts and not having a power of attorney
which is, shall we say, complete, may well cause
problems.
MR COLE:  Thank you for that.
PRESIDENT:  Dr Abdulla, would like to say anything?
DR TALEB:  I agree with Adrian.  We have discussed this.
I do agree, have the same opinions.
PRESIDENT:  So for the sake of today as well, and for
this hearing, I think, if I may, so the tribunal will
allow Mr Stephen Burke to continue with his
presentation and representing his client.
Now, we're going to discuss in my time with --
during the break, whether we're going to need a
further power of attorney or not, just for covering
those aspects of the Bahraini court as the respondent
counsel has just referred to.  But we'll come back to
you with this at a moment.
I don't want to waste too much time on this, but
we need to get in the respondent application as soon
as we can because we have to deal with this matter.
Thank you.
So now, this is for the respondent to raise his
objections and to hear from him regarding the
application made on 18th May.
Application
MR WYGAS:  In relation to the application on the date of
18th May -- I'm just getting the relevant documents
up.
The respondent has seen the tribunal's directions
in relation to timing and the respondent has provided
two sets of submissions.  We've not heard back from
the claimant in response to those submissions,
particularly, the claimant did not take the
opportunity that the tribunal gave them to put in
further submissions on 28th May.
So if I may, I will keep my submissions short, so
to keep time in reply to deal with what the claimant
says in relation to the detailed points.
I'll therefore make five quick points, if I may.
The first is the extent of the breach.
The second is the alleged compliance with
procedural order 2.
The third is the requirement for proper
instructions to the experts.
The fourth is the failure to show any remorse
and/or acceptance of the position at all.
And the fifth is the serious prejudice caused.
In relation to the extent of the breach, so you
will have seen from the submissions dated 28th May
that there are 1,868 new documents, and that is out of
the 2,331 which the experts rely upon.
So 84 per cent of the documents have only been
provided to Ms Rampersad.  And I focus on Ms Rampersad
for obvious reasons, given that the vast majority of
the new documents relate to her or relate to quantum
and do not relate to delay.
The timing of the expert reports was tied to the
hearing.  So it seems that the provision of the
documents with the experts' reports was timed
purposefully to be as late as possible.
There is no explanation for the delay, and there's
not even an attempt to provide an explanation.
Therefore, in my submission, this should be taken
as a considered, cynical attempt to provide
information to TTSJV's own experts as late -- whilst
delaying the provision of those documents to DTC's
experts until as late as they possibly could.  That is
clearly, in my submission, a serious breach.
As to the second point, the claimant relies on
alleged compliance with procedural order 2.  In my
submission, that is obviously and clearly nonsense,
for the reasons that have already been given.
In effect, what the claimant says is that under
procedural order 2, factual evidence can be provided
as late as possible and it can be provided with expert
evidence in the run-up to the hearing.  That is
clearly not what procedural order 2 meant, and that
ignores the dates set out in procedural order 2 for
the provision of factual evidence.
As to the third point, and the requirement for
proper instructions for experts, again, the tribunal
will have seen reference to cases like ICI.  In that
case, Fraser J, as he was then, says experts of like
discipline should have access to the same material.
No party should provide its own expert evidence -- its
own independent expert with material which is not
available to his or her opposite number.
That is precisely not what the claimant has done
in this case.  And clearly those obligations apply in
this arbitration, given the seat is in London and
there are obligations to conduct the arbitration in
good faith, as the respondent has set out in its
application.
In relation to the issue of remorse or trying to
deal with this matter, can I just take you to
This is an email from Addleshaw Goddard and dated
9th May.  The second paragraph, this is correspondence
between the parties' representatives in relation to
the issue of the very late provision of the documents
to the experts, or to TTSJV's experts, and this is in
response to DTC saying, well, we need to understand
where these documents are in the bundle.
Addleshaw Goddard say this:
"As all the relevant documentation has been
provided in compliance with Procedural Order No 2, it
is already 'on the record'."
Well, sir, you have my submissions in relation to
that:
"It would serve only to waste costs (and to
prejudice the Claimant's hearing preparation) ..."
So clearly, Addleshaw Goddard understands that
trying to index or identify documents does clearly
prejudice hearing preparation.  And the email goes on:
"... to require the Claimant to cross-reference
that documentation to prior exhibit numbers,
particularly as the hearing bundle is now 'live' ...
There is no reason why the Respondent cannot spend its
own time and money doing that exercise, however, if it
believes that would serve any useful purpose."
So when the issue was raised with TTSJV, there was
a flat refusal for it to assist in any way in
identifying the new documents which have been
provided.  It could have helped by simply saying,
well, around 90 per cent of the documents are new.
But it didn't say that.  And it was only on 28th May
that the respondent was able to identify with
precision the new documents.
And you've seen from the submissions on 28th May
why that took so long, given the problems with the
indexing of the documents.
So then, onto the issue of prejudice.  The
prejudice caused is obvious.  If you have, as in
claim 1, more than 9 out of 10 documents being new,
and provided to the claimant's experts so that they
have time to consider them, but not provided to the
defendant's experts so they have a similar amount of
time to consider them, it is obvious that that will
cause serious and substantial prejudice.
Having said that, the respondent has been
reasonable and doesn't simply throw its hands up and
say that the whole position is untenable, which in my
submission would not be an unacceptable stance to
take.
Instead, the respondent considered the position
carefully, taking the extra time to do so, which
further prejudiced the respondent.
However, that extra time has led to the respondent
identifying the heads of claim and evidence which are
impacted by the new documents, as set out in the
respondent's submissions of 28th May.
That shows two main points, both of which add to
the prejudice that the respondent has suffered by the
claimant's actions.
The first is that the documents effectively all
relate to quantum, so the burden of reviewing them all
falls on Mr Barry.
The second is, as I've already mentioned, that
less than 1 in 10 documents in relation to claim 1
have been provided previously.
So in relation to the largest head of claim, TTSJV
is trying to bring that claim whilst sitting on
93 per cent of its documents until the final moments.
Given that, in my submission, the right way to
deal with the prejudice, as set out in the submissions
dated 28th May, is for the claimant not to be able to
rely on the new documents in relation to claims 1, 3,
It was hoped that TTSJV would be helpful and
identify which parts of its expert evidence relied on
the new documents, as was requested by the respondent.
It's decided not to do that.  Frankly, it's just
straight refused.
Given that, the only option is that the expert
evidence of Ms Rampersad in relation to claims 1, 3,
4, 6 and 7 must be struck out, because there is no way
of identifying which parts of that evidence relates to
the new documents, and which parts of that evidence
relates to the documents which were provided in
accordance with procedural order number 2.
So those are my initial submissions in relation to
the application.  And if I may, I'll reply to what
Mr Burke has got to say in relation to this.
PRESIDENT:  Yes, Mr Burke, please go ahead.
MR BURKE:  Thank you, sir.
The application and the submissions you've heard
this morning are long on hyperbole and short on
substance.  They start from a premise that is clearly
wrong.  They depend on prejudice that has been
patently manufactured, and they conclude with an
updated prayer for relief that is not simply
draconian, it is an absurd overreach which exposes the
true motivation for the application.  And I will take
those points in order.
First, the entire premise of the application is
wrong.  It rests on the presumption that there was
some restriction against the experts providing the
further documents upon which they rely with their
reports; or alternatively, it rests on there having
been some obligation on the claimant or its experts
previously to have provided those documents.  Neither
is right or, frankly, even close to being right.
I have set out the key provisions of procedural
order number 2 in my written submissions.  The key
part here is at paragraph 69 in procedural order
number 2.  That is at {B1.6-13}.  We don't need to
turn it up.
That provides expert reports must comply with
article 5(2) of the IBA Rules and article 5(2)(e) of
the IBA Rules provides in terms that the documents on
which the party expert relies, party-appointed expert
relies, that have not been submitted -- it's not
already have been submitted -- shall be provided with
his or her report, and that is at {J123}.
But that language could not be any clearer.  The
IBA Rules, which are incorporated into these
proceedings via procedural order number 2, not only
permit an expert to produce documents upon which she
relies with her report, they require it.
And just pausing there, I'm not sure why any of
this should come as a surprise to the respondent.
This is standard practice in arbitration proceedings.
Now, the tribunal obviously doesn't need to take
my word for that.  They will bring their own
experience to bear.  But the fact that procedural
order number 2 simply reflects the IBA Rules itself
makes that proposition self-evident.
Now, even this morning, we've had two rounds of
written submissions and now oral submissions in
support of the application.  Even this morning, there
is not one attempt made to explain why that is wrong.
It is simply asserted to be obviously wrong.
Now, in my learned friend's written submissions of
28th May, he suggested he would make good the
proposition that it was wrong, with reference to
paragraphs 42 to 54 to procedural order number 2.
Now, I don't know whether he intends tactically to
withhold those submissions until the replies so that I
can't respond to them, but I'll deal with them in
short order in any event, because those paragraphs
provide absolutely no assistance whatsoever for the
application.
First, before I do that, let me understand what
I think the premise of my learned friend's position is
going to be, because I have to guess, because he's yet
to articulate it.  I anticipate -- the anticipation is
that the premise will be that the document production
regime somehow means that we were required to produce
the documents upon which Ms Rampersad relies, during
the document production phase of the arbitration.  So
when documents were produced in accordance with the
document production phase, we were supposed to have
produced those documents to the respondent.
Now, of course, that is not what paragraph 9 --
paragraph 69 of the procedural order number 2 says.
It does not say that expert reports should contain the
documents on which party-appointed experts rely that
have not already been submitted, but they're only
allowed to do so if they're on the record or they've
been produced in document production.
Second, the respondent's new argument, if it ever
is articulated, will ignore what the document
production regime actually says.  It has been referred
to repeatedly in written submissions as a disclosure
regime.  And of course, that is wrong.
The document production regime in procedural order
number 2 is for the production of specific documents,
or narrow and specific categories of documents,
production of which is sought and ordered in the
parties' respective Redfern schedules.  There's no
obligation on either party to produce documents
unilaterally.  Indeed, there's no permission for
documents to be produced unilaterally, because
document production has to be made against specific
requests, and that is set out at paragraph 53 of
procedural order number 2.
And any attempt to rely on paragraphs 42 to 54 to
procedural order number 2 will run into paragraph 51
of procedural order number 2.
And it might be worth bringing that up on the
screen.  That's {B1.6-10}.  And this provides that
documents that are exchanged in document production
are not on the record.  They're only on the record if
they are subsequently filed as exhibits to any witness
statement, written submission or expert report.
So what this does is it provides a restriction on
the parties seeking later to deploy evidence that has
been produced in document production without it having
first been produced on the record by way of attachment
to written submissions, witness statements or expert
reports.
But it's clear from this, of course, that
documents produced with expert reports are on the
record.  And it's also clear that the restriction here
is against the deployment of documents used in
document production that have not previously been
deployed.
It is not against experts producing documents that
are attached to their reports, and that is provided in
terms of paragraph 69 of procedural order number 2.
I'll come back to this shortly in the context of
the instructions that have been given to my learned
friend's experts.
And again, none of this is unique or experimental.
This is not an unusual document production regime in
LCIA arbitration.  This is absolutely standard
practice.
Now, I also say that any attempt to rely on these
provisions of procedural order number 2 would not just
be new, it would be wholly contrived.  And the reason
I say that is because it's inconsistent with the
instructions that have been given to my learned
friend's experts.
If we could look at Mr Barry's reply report, we
can see that.  That's at {D5.19-12}, paragraph 2.
Next page, 13.
We see here -- sorry, could you just zoom out so
we can see the whole page, please?  Yeah.
So we have a statement here by Mr Barry of his
instructions and he says, paragraph 2.14, that his
instructions were, his instructions and understanding
were -- sorry, could we just stay out on the full
page, please?
Instruction and understanding were, and he then
quotes from joint statement 1.  He says:
"Mr Barry understands that only the documents in
evidence or on the record can be relied upon for any
Expert assessment and opinion."
And then, in case that's not clear as to what his
instructions were, he provides the clarity at
paragraph 2.16, and that's the last sentence.  He says
that:
"My instructions are to only rely on the
supporting documents exhibited to the parties'
pleadings and the factual witness statements."
So what Mr Barry is saying here is that his
instructions were that he was not entitled to rely on
documents that were produced during document
production; he was only entitled to rely on documents
that were provided as exhibits to pleadings or witness
statements.
We could have produced the entire suite of
documents that are now being complained about with
document production last year, and presumably Mr Barry
would have ignored them, because they were his
instructions.
So even on its face, there is a disconnect between
the premise -- at least the premise that was put in
writing -- and what is now said to be the application.
And that applies equally in response to the
allegations of bad faith that my friend has made.  He
suggests that we should have produced these documents
to Mr Barry at the same time as we provided them to
our own expert.
Now, of course, nothing in procedural order
number 2 says that, or even close.  But if we had done
that, Mr Barry would presumably have ignored them,
because his instructions were to only rely on
documents that were exhibited to the parties'
pleadings or to the witness statements.
And so I'm afraid the inconsistency here just
exposes the real nature of the application.
Before I come on to the issue of the manufactured
prejudice, I do want to just touch very briefly on
English High Court authorities that my learned friend
has referred to in writing.
I'm grateful for his admission that this is a
London seat arbitration.  My objection is not that
these authorities are English; it is that they are
authorities that relate specifically to the
presentation of expert evidence in the English courts.
That is an entirely different exercise with different
principles and different procedural rules to those
that apply in arbitration.
The decisions in the two cases that my learned
friend has cited tell us nothing about how evidence in
international arbitration proceedings, under the LCIA
rules, is to be taken, particularly given that in
arbitration there is no duty of disclosure.
In fact, if we look at the basis of the exercise,
if we look at what happened in the Dana UK case, the
evidence was excluded in that case because there were
found to have been breaches of a specific pretrial
review order that was made, and then of Part 35 and
practice direction to Part 35 of the Civil Procedure
Rules.  And the guidance for the instruction of
experts in civil claims, which is referenced in that
practice direction.
None of that has any application in these
arbitration proceedings.
I appreciate that my learned friend was counsel in
the Dana UK case, and I don't intend to debate the
facts of that case with him, but I was also surprised
at what he said about the relevance of that
application in his written submissions.
This is at paragraph 52 of the submissions that
were filed on Thursday.  We don't need to turn it up,
but I will quote it directly.
He said:
"In this case, the position is worse than the case
of Dana.  In that case, documents were provided to the
experts by the client.  And so there was maybe some
excuse for those documents not being provided to the
other side immediately."
Well, I've read that decision, and that is the
opposite of the finding in that case.  Indeed, one of
the primary grounds upon which the party was found to
have been in breach was because documents had been
provided by the client directly to the expert, without
the party's solicitors having a role, so without them
being able to tell what had and had not been provided.
And that's set out in terms at paragraph 56 of the
judgment.  And that's a {J122-15}.
And of course, the premise of the decision in the
Dana UK case was based expressly upon procedural rules
that have no application here.
And so that is why I say that should be the end of
this application.  There is no, frankly, even
articulated breach as at this point in time, let alone
a breach that stands credible analysis when put
against the terms of procedural rule number 2, and
because there is no breach, issues of prejudice really
don't arise.
But if the tribunal is minded to consider the
issue of prejudice, it can only conclude that that
prejudice has been manufactured for entirely tactical
reasons.
I've set out the reasons for that in my written
submissions, and it is notable that my learned
friend's written submissions on the 28th, and the
submissions that were made in this morning, make no
attempt at all to engage with any of that.
As I said in my written submissions, the relevant
evidence was provided with -- the vast majority of it
was provided with -- first round expert reports on 7th
April.  And yet it was then not until 8th May, more
than a full month later, that any issue was taken with
that evidence by the respondent.  And it was not then
until 18th May, less than two weeks before today, that
the application was filed.
And the only excuse I can see that's even been
offered for that delay is to claim that the respondent
couldn't even try and identify what was new before it
had the hearing bundle, apparently because it would
need to look across more than one index, and because
it would need to search metadata.
Now, I'm unclear how that situation would have
been any different if we'd produced all this evidence
in document production, because the same exercise
would still have been required.  But given that the
respondent has had the agreed expert -- the agreed
hearing bundle index since 4th April, so three days
before first round expert reports were filed, even the
factual premise of that justification simply does not
work.
PRESIDENT:  Mr Burke, just a question about time.  So we
need to give Mr Luke some time to reply, then the
tribunal have to make --
MR BURKE:  Yes, I understood I had 30 minutes.  I think
I've had 18 so far.
PRESIDENT:  Oh, right.  Okay.
MR BURKE:  I can take the rest of it relatively briefly.
The premise of the application, the justification
that's given for the delay, is also really quite
extraordinary.  It must have been obvious to the
respondent within days of receiving the first round
expert report, that there were documents that its
expert had not seen before.
If they were acting in good faith, if this was a
serious application, they would have raised the issue
then so it could have been dealt with.  But not only
did the respondent choose not to do that, it has at no
point attempted to explain why.
And so what we've really come down to is
this: what the respondent has taken the last two
months to do, at least this is what it claims it's
taken the last two months to do, is to identify what
they think is new.  An exercise they claim has taken
two full months.
If we look at Mr Barry's presentation, we can see
it would have taken him substantially less time simply
to have reviewed the documents for the purposes of his
analysis.  And that, I say, is, in itself, fatal to
the application.  It establishes that the prejudice
that's now relied on is entirely manufactured by the
respondent's delay.
I won't comment now on the presentation.  Of
course, we received that at just after 11 o'clock last
night, and so we've had no opportunity to review it.
I would say that it's apparent from what Mr Barry
says that he's taking a rather different approach to
the analysis of evidence now than he did in his own
first round report.
And I say that because in his first round report,
he was perfectly happy -- this is before any new
evidence was provided -- he was perfectly happy to
take a sampling approach in the context of head of
claim 1.  He says that in terms at paragraph 37 of his
first report, that's at {D4.69-14}.  It appears now
that he's no longer prepared to do that when it
doesn't allow procedural advantage.
I'll say very briefly a few words on remedy.  The
remedy that's sought is not just extraordinary, it is
absurd.  It has morphed from a nebulous relief in the
original application now to a strikeout application in
respect of my client's quantum expert's opinions on
most of its heads of claim.
And if I can illustrate just how extraordinary
that is with reference to one of those heads of claim.
That is head of claim 3.  The only new documents about
which complaint is taken in respect of head of claim 3
are proofs of payment.  Even on Mr Barry's leisurely
assessment, it would take a day to review those proofs
of payment.
The idea that the entirety of Ms Rampersad's
